nodes.summary:
- Module 6: dual-mode offline knowledge-graph viewer (3d-force-graph)
  graph-viewer/generate_viewer.py reads graphify-out/graph.json and
  writes a single self-contained graphify-out/graph-3d-viewer.html --
  library and graph data both inlined, no fetch()/imports/CDN, same
  single-file philosophy as ultron-dashboard.html. Not a live Flask page
  (step 27 explicitly skips that); a regenerated static artifact, same
  pattern graphify's own graph.html already uses.
  Privacy inherited, not reimplemented: this only ever reads whatever's
  currently in graph.json, so a Module-4-redacted private node arrives
  here already reduced to {id, label:"[private]", category, community,
  timestamps} -- no separate privacy logic needed, and none written.
  Three modes, verified live in Chrome (screenshots + console-error
  checks for each): Clean (2D, settled, default), Explore 3D (full 3D,
  slow auto-rotate, free orbit/pan/zoom), List (plain sortable table) --
  per step 24, the animated 3D view is deliberately never the only way to
  read the graph. Human-facing features from step 25, all confirmed
  working rather than just written: color by category (+ a distinct
  muted grey overriding category color for any private node), node size
  by connection count, hover tooltip with dates/tags/community, search
  that dims (not hides) non-matches so the graph's overall shape stays
  visible while filtering.
  Vendored (Module 5's "downloaded once, no CDN" pattern):
  3d-force-graph v1.80.0 from unpkg -- bundles its own internal three.js
  copy (self-contained UMD build), deliberately separate from
  three-pipeline's three.module.js/three.core.js, which Module 9's hero
  head uses instead; the library's UMD build doesn't support bringing
  your own three.js instance, so two vendored copies is correct here, not
  duplication to clean up.
  Step 22: confirmed (already established in Module 2's gap spec) that
  graphify already outputs Obsidian-native markdown/wikilinks
  (graphify-out/obsidian/) -- noted for reference, doesn't replace this
  viewer, since Obsidian's own graph view has no 3D/physics mode.
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XboKnCsJJkFsyaDR3eh5he
- Module 5: vendor Three.js locally, install and verify Blender's headless pipeline
  Shared setup for Module 6 (knowledge-graph viewer) and Module 9 (hero
  robotic head) -- doesn't build either feature, just proves the two
  prerequisites they'll both depend on actually work.
  - three-pipeline/three.module.js + three.core.js: three.js r186
    (0.186.0), vendored from unpkg (downloaded once, not a runtime CDN
    load -- Module 6 wants this fully offline). Real bug hit building
    this: three.js's build/ splits into a thin three.module.js re-export
    wrapper and the actual implementation in three.core.js, which it
    imports via a relative path -- vendoring only the first file fails
    with a generic "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module" error
    that never names the actual missing dependency. Both files required
    together, documented in three-pipeline/README.md.
  - three-pipeline/smoke_test.html: verified live in Chrome (served over
    a local HTTP server -- ES module imports are blocked under file://
    by CORS) -- a real THREE.Scene/WebGLRenderer/Mesh rendered one frame,
    confirmed via both the page's own reported revision/renderer state
    and a visible rendered cube.
  - Blender 5.2.1 LTS installed (winget). three-pipeline/blender_smoke_test.py
    proves the actual mechanism Module 9 will use: a bpy script run
    headlessly via `blender --background --python ...`, constructing
    geometry procedurally and exporting a real .glb -- verified by
    checking the output's glTF magic bytes, not just that a file exists.
  - Confirmed the dashboard is not React-based (single-file vanilla
    HTML/JS, no build step), so the roadmap's React Three Fiber clause
    doesn't apply -- plain Three.js as a native ES module matches the
    existing codebase.
  Deliberately not done: not wired into ultron-dashboard.html (that's
  Module 6/9's own work), no Sketchfab/Poly Haven placeholder model
  downloaded (the roadmap's fallback for if the Blender pipeline hit
  trouble -- it didn't).
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XboKnCsJJkFsyaDR3eh5he
- Module 3: audit git history for secrets (clean), add gitleaks as a mandatory pre-commit gate
  Full-history scan (85 commits, gitleaks v8.30.1, local/free) found no
  real secrets -- 2 findings, both verified false positives (minified
  third-party Obsidian plugin JS, and graphify's own SHA-256 content-hash
  cache). Targeted checks beyond the generic ruleset confirmed .env and
  *.db were never committed at any point. Full findings and methodology
  in GIT-SECRET-AUDIT.md.
  Given nothing real was found, step 7's git filter-repo history rewrite
  is deliberately NOT performed -- it's conditional on finding something
  to remove, and running a destructive, force-pushed rewrite (which would
  need its own separate explicit confirmation regardless) to fix a
  problem that doesn't exist isn't the right call. git-filter-repo is
  installed and ready if a future audit ever finds something real.
  Ongoing gate: .gitleaks.toml (path-scoped allowlist for the two
  verified false positives -- deliberately not a content/regex allowlist,
  which would also hide a real hex-shaped secret) + .githooks/pre-commit,
  activated via `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` (tracked in
  .githooks/ rather than the untracked .git/hooks/, so it actually
  travels with a clone -- documented in GIT-SECRET-AUDIT.md that this
  needs re-running once per fresh clone). Fails closed if gitleaks isn't
  installed. Verified both directions: a realistic fake secret was
  genuinely blocked (exit 1, no commit created), and this very commit
  passed the same live gate cleanly.
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XboKnCsJJkFsyaDR3eh5he
- Fix + document: graphify's own rebuild silently reverts code-derived private nodes to plaintext
  Found immediately after merging Module 4 to main: the post-checkout
  hook's code rebuild re-extracts AST nodes from source files without
  any awareness of visibility, and merges them back into graph.json by
  matching source_file -- a freshly re-extracted node has its real label/
  source_file again, so it overwrites a redacted stub outright, visibility
  field included. Confirmed live: one git checkout dropped the private
  count from 48 to 19 (every code-derived private node reverted to
  plaintext; document-derived ones survived, since the code rebuild never
  touches those). Nothing was pushed in that state -- caught and fixed
  before this commit by re-running graph-schema/run.ps1, which correctly
  re-catches and re-redacts them from their restored plaintext content.
  GRAPH-SCHEMA-DESIGN.md corrected: the "sticky once private" guarantee
  only holds within enrich_visibility.py's own reruns, not against
  graphify's independent rebuild process, which can and does transiently
  restore plaintext until the privacy scripts are re-run. Real safety
  boundary is "committed to git after verifying," not "graph.json
  currently looks redacted."
  85 nodes now classified private (up from 48, reflecting both graph
  growth across rebuilds and better keyword coverage on freshly-restored
  plaintext content) -- verified zero leaking content, zero leaks in the
  regenerated GRAPH_REPORT.md, before this commit.
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XboKnCsJJkFsyaDR3eh5he
- Add graph-schema/run.ps1 and document the hook-reopens-the-leak finding
  Confirmed live: committing Module 4 itself triggered graphify's own
  post-commit hook, which regenerated GRAPH_REPORT.md/graph.html with
  graphify's own leaky community-naming, silently reopening the exact
  leak safe_report.py had just closed -- no automatic trigger re-closes
  it. run.ps1 chains enrich_visibility.py + safe_report.py (right
  interpreters, right order) into one command to lower the chance of
  forgetting; GRAPH-SCHEMA-DESIGN.md now documents this as the single
  most important operational gotcha in the design.
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XboKnCsJJkFsyaDR3eh5he
- Module 4: per-node timestamps/tags/visibility + encryption at rest for private nodes
  Implements the gap KNOWLEDGE-GRAPH-GAP-SPEC.md (Module 2) found, as a
  post-processing layer over graphify's own graph.json -- not a fork of
  it. New graph-schema/ directory:
  - enrich_visibility.py: adds category/tags/date_created/date_updated/
    visibility to every node. visibility defaults private on any doubt
    (broad keyword + IP-pattern match against the roadmap's explicit
    hard-private list), and enforcement is real: a private node's full
    content is removed from the plaintext graph.json entirely (only an
    opaque stub with id/community/timestamps remains) and stored,
    Fernet-encrypted, in graphify-out/private-nodes.enc.json -- gitignored
    even though it's encrypted, per Module 9's own "private nodes should
    never enter public repo history" rule; encryption is defense in
    depth, not a license to commit it. Key lives in .env (already
    gitignored), generated once, no recovery path if lost.
  - Two real bugs found and fixed during development, both now covered by
    graph-schema/test_enrich.py:
    1. A naive first version reclassified already-redacted private nodes
       as public on a second run, because the redaction itself removes
       the keywords that triggered private classification. Fixed by
       recovering the decrypted original before re-deriving anything, and
       making "private" sticky once set.
    2. graphify's own community auto-naming derives a community's label
       from its most-connected node -- since a node's id necessarily
       still contains its real name (ids can't be redacted without
       breaking every edge), a private node's identity was leaking back
       in through its community's name in GRAPH_REPORT.md/graph.html even
       though the node's own label correctly read "[private]". Fixed by
       graph-schema/safe_report.py, which forces any community touching a
       private node to a generic name before regenerating those files.
       Verified by grepping the regenerated report/html for real private
       content after the fix -- zero hits.
  - graphify-out/tag-index.json: the standalone {tag: [node_ids]} index
    the roadmap asked retrieval code be able to query directly.
  - GRAPH-SCHEMA-DESIGN.md: the versioned schema doc, including what's
    NOT solved tonight (doesn't retroactively scrub git history -- that's
    Module 3's job; not wired into graphify's own hook; no manual
    un-flag-false-positive tool yet).
  Run against the real project graph: 491 nodes, 48 classified private
  (trade/FIFO/portfolio code, token/credential-handling functions,
  Tailscale and Pi-setup docs) -- reviewed the full list by hand before
  committing, looked correctly calibrated, not wildly over- or
  under-broad.
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XboKnCsJJkFsyaDR3eh5he
- Module 2: scan for beta results, document graphify's real schema, spec the gap
  Read-only investigation, no code changes -- gates Module 4 per the
  roadmap ("do not proceed until this spec exists").
  - Searched BETA-TESTERS.md/CODE-AUDIT.md/BETA-LAUNCH-CHECKLIST.md and
    queried the graph itself for recorded beta results: roster is empty,
    one self-test exists (2026-09-13, owner's own second device), its

  - Inspected graph.json/manifest.json/cost.json/the obsidian export
    directly rather than assuming graphify's format -- documented the

- Module 1: fix TTS delay proportional to reply length (stream instead of buffer)
  Fish Audio's own /v1/tts already streams via chunked transfer, but both
  ends of our own pipe defeated it: _fish_audio_tts called resp.read() and
  waited for the entire reply before returning, and the dashboard's
  speakReply() called res.blob() which equally waits for the whole fetch
  to finish before doing anything. Net effect: audio start time scaled
  with reply length exactly as reported, even though the audio itself was
  always being generated progressively on Fish Audio's end the whole time.
  - _fish_audio_tts now returns a chunk generator (resp.read(8192) in a
    loop) instead of pre-read bytes; the /api/tts route forwards it via
    Flask's stream_with_context instead of building one Response body.
  - Dashboard: speakReply() now uses MediaSource + SourceBuffer to feed
    chunks to <audio> as they arrive (checked via
    MediaSource.isTypeSupported first, with the old blob-based approach
    kept as a fallback for browsers where that's false). A plain <audio
    src="...">  can't send the Authorization header this endpoint needs,
    which is why this needs fetch()+MSE rather than just pointing an
    element at the URL directly.
  Verified two ways:
